question: Several hours after vaginal delivery, a male newborn delivered at full-term develops tachycardia and tachypnea. His blood pressure is within normal limits. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 79% in the right hand and 61% in the left foot. Physical examination shows bluish discoloration of the face and trunk, supraclavicular and intercostal retractions, and a machine-like murmur over the precordium. Bedside echocardiography shows pulmonary and systemic circulation are in parallel rather than in series. What is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy for this patient?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Parallel pulmonary and systemic circulation" -> "Right-to-left shunting of blood" -> "Cyanosis and hypoxemia" -> "Pulmonary hypertension" -> "Increased pulmonary vascular resistance" -> "Alprostadil" -> 85%
CHAIN: "Tachycardia and tachypnea in a newborn" -> "Cyanosis and hypoxemia" -> "Right-to-left shunting of blood" -> "Alprostadil" -> 80%
analysis: The clinical presentation and findings described are consistent with a diagnosis of persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN). In this condition, there is failure of the normal circulatory transition that occurs after birth, leading to persistent elevation of pulmonary vascular resistance. The most appropriate pharmacotherapy for this patient is Alprostadil, a prostaglandin E1 analog that helps to maintain patency of the ductus arteriosus and improve pulmonary blood flow.
